lessons.title: The year end, and what it draws on
lessons.html:
Every chapter so far stops at the month. This one is about what those months become, because the client's annual accounts, tax filing and any audit all draw on exactly the work described in this module.

What changes at year end, and it is less than people expect. The same closing discipline, applied once more, with three additions: everything is looked at across twelve months rather than one, balances are confirmed rather than reconciled, and somebody outside the process reads it.

Confirming rather than reconciling. A monthly reconciliation proves the ledger agrees with a statement. Year end asks a harder question of every balance sheet line: what is this, and can it be evidenced? Receivables against a schedule and the client's confirmation of who genuinely owes; stock against a count; loans against a lender's statement; the asset register against reality. A balance carried for twelve months without that question being asked is where the surprises live.

What the twelve-month read finds that a monthly read does not. A control account that never quite cleared. An accrual reversed in one month and re-raised in the next. A prepayment schedule that stopped being run in August. None of these is visible in the month it happens; all are obvious across a year.

Preparing the file. Whoever prepares the annual accounts — the client's auditor, a tax adviser, the firm — needs the same things every time: the trial balance, the reconciliations, the schedules behind every material balance, and the explanations. A unit that has done its monthly work properly assembles this in a day. One that has not spends weeks, at a cost somebody pays.

What the bookkeeper owns and does not. You own the records being complete, reconciled and evidenced. You do not own the tax computation, the accounting policy judgements or the accounts themselves — those sit with whoever is engaged for them. Knowing that boundary before the year-end conversation starts is what keeps you from being asked, in good faith, to decide something that is not yours.

What the client experiences, and why it matters commercially. A year end that arrives as a short list of confirmations is a client who renews without thinking about it. One that arrives as weeks of requests, reconstructions and surprises is a client who starts wondering what they have been paying for — and the difference between those two experiences was decided across twelve unremarkable months, not in the fortnight anybody is looking.

And the habit that makes year end unremarkable. Ask the confirming question once a quarter rather than once a year, on the two or three balances that carry the most. Four small conversations across the year replace one long uncomfortable one, and nothing is discovered eleven months after it could have been fixed.

m4.desc: Confidentiality with scenarios, the client voice with verbatim rewrites, the bad-news protocol, both chairs of review, and reading your own numbers.

lessons.title: Confidentiality — the walls, tested
lessons.html:
Every client room is a sealed vessel; the rules are absolute because the temptations are ordinary. Four scenarios, decided:

1. The benchmark request. Cascade's MD, friendly, over a call: "You do Bellamy too — what do retailers like them spend on POS charges? Just a range." The range IS Bellamy's data wearing a disguise. Answer from public knowledge only ("card commissions in Nigeria typically run 0.5–0.75%; let's look at YOURS") — and note the refusal shape: give something useful and general, so the no doesn't feel like a wall.

2. The helpful shortcut. Chidinma (Bellamy's bookkeeper-side contact) WhatsApps you asking for last month's P&L "quickly, the MD is asking". The document is theirs; the CHANNEL is the breach. "Sending it to your Documents now — it'll be in the portal in one minute." Client materials travel the logged rails even when the recipient is entitled to them; a personal-channel habit, once formed, will eventually carry something it must not.

3. The dinner story. A client's books contained something genuinely funny, no names needed. Not told. Lagos, at the level our clients live, is one degree of separation — and the storyteller who is careful with names is still teaching the table that our clients' insides are entertainment. The reputation cost lands on the unit, not the anecdote.

4. The device. Statements and exports on your laptop are transit, not archive: they live in the Hub, and local copies go when the task does. Screens lock when you stand; client tabs close before screen-shares; and the household rule applies — family seeing a client's name on your screen is already a leak, however loving the household.

Confidentiality is not a policy we comply with; it is the product. Clients hand us the most private thing a business has, and the fee is paid because the handover is safe. The breach that ends a career is rarely dramatic — a screenshot to the wrong chat, an open laptop, a story told well. Boring discipline is the whole game.

DRILL: A prospective client asks, as a test: "Who else do you keep books for?" What may you say? House policy [red-pen]: named references only with the referenced client's standing consent; otherwise sector-level ("retail, food, logistics") and the offer to arrange a reference call. The instinct to impress with names is the instinct to manage.

The fifth scenario, which is the one that actually happens. Nobody asks. You are on a call about Cascade and you mention, harmlessly, that another retail client had the same problem with their POS provider last quarter. You have named no one and disclosed no figure — and you have told Cascade's MD that you talk about clients on calls. Everything after that is heard differently, including the things you do not say.

What confidentiality protects that is not the data. The client's willingness to tell you things. A bookkeeper who is told about the difficult month before it appears in the numbers can do their job; one the client manages information toward cannot. Discretion is the condition of being useful, rather than a constraint on it.

And the household case. Working from home, on a shared machine, on a call somebody else can hear. The rules that are obvious in an office are the ones most often lost remotely, and they are the same rules: screens not visible, calls not overheard, files not on a personal drive, and nothing about a client in a message to somebody who is not on the engagement.

lessons.title: The client voice — five rewrites, verbatim
lessons.html:
To your clients you ARE the firm; every message teaches them what the service is like. The register: warm, plain, unhurried, never defensive; help-shaped, never accusation-shaped. Five real situations, bad and good, word for word:

1. The unexplained transaction.
✗ "You didn't tell us what the 230k cheque to Musa Ent was for. We can't do your books like this."
✓ "Could you help us place one item — a cheque to Musa Ent, ₦230,000, on the 9th? Once we know what it was for, July is fully posted."
The good version asks for help, names the specifics, and shows the payoff of answering.

2. The chronically late statement.
✗ "As usual we still don't have your GTB statement."
✓ "We're one document away from starting your close — the GTB statement for July. Could Tunde send it today? The earlier it lands, the earlier your statements do."
"As usual" wins an argument and loses a client; the good version converts frustration into a deadline the client can act on.

3. The client who wants the impossible.
✗ "That's not how accounting works."
✓ "There's a cleaner way to get what you're after. If we post it the way you've described, your VAT return overstates — which costs you real money. Here's what I'd suggest instead…"
Never make the client feel foolish; make the better path feel like THEIR win (because it is).

4. The scope drift.
✗ "We don't do that."
✓ "Happy to help with that — it sits outside your current service, so let me have our team add it properly with a small fee adjustment. That way it's covered every month, not just this once."
The no becomes a yes-with-structure; the tier conversation (M1) in its natural habitat.

5. The angry message. Client, 21:40: "Third time asking about this!!! Is anyone actually working on our account???"
✗ (at 21:41) "We replied on Tuesday, please check your portal."
✓ (next working morning, 08:40) "You're right to expect better tracking from us, and I'm sorry this felt dropped. Here's where each of your three items stands: [three lines]. The second one is waiting on the bank's response — I'll chase them this morning and update you by noon."
Note everything the good version does: waits for working hours (the after-hours notice covered the night; answering at 21:41 teaches a service level we don't sell), opens with validation not evidence, itemises, owns the next action WITH a time. You may be right on the facts and still wrong in the reply.

The channel rule underneath all five: queries through Follow-ups, documents through requests, everything else in the room — and any material thing settled by voice gets a same-day room summary, because a decision that exists only in a phone call doesn't exist.

DRILL: Rewrite this real specimen: "We noticed you again mixed personal and business spending. This makes our work very difficult." — One good answer: "A few July items look personal (list attached, ₦184,000 total) — should we treat these as drawings as before? If it helps, a separate card for business spend would make your statements cleaner and your tax position safer." Names the facts, offers the mechanism, gives the client a dignified path.

lessons.title: Bad news — the protocol, walked
lessons.html:
Something will eventually go wrong: a statement will be late, an error will reach a delivered pack, a statutory date will be at risk. The protocol is identical for all three: early, plainly, cause attached, path forward, before the system's surfaces tell them first.

Walk the late statement. It's the 4th working day; Bellamy's GTB pages for the 28th–31st are still missing despite two chases. The deadline is tomorrow and you will miss it. The message goes TODAY:

"Your July statements will be one day late — we're missing the GTB pages for the 28th–31st, which we've requested twice (most recently this morning). The moment they arrive we need about three hours; if Tunde can send them today, we may still make Friday. Everything else is closed and reviewed."

Anatomy: the news first (no burying), the cause (specific, not defensive), the client's lever (Tunde, today), the honest new promise, and the reassurance that is TRUE (the rest is done). What it never contains: "unfortunately due to circumstances", blame theatrics, or a promise you can't keep to soften the moment.

Walk the discovered error. August 12th, you find July's delivered pack overstated repairs by ₦230,000 (a suspense repost missed the reversal). The instinct to quietly fix it in August is the career-shaping mistake. The sequence: reviewer first (same hour), agreed correction, then the client — "We found an error in July's delivered statements: repairs were overstated by ₦230,000, profit correspondingly understated. Corrected statements are in your Documents; the cause was a duplicated posting on our side, and we've added a check so it can't recur." Clients forgive errors admitted at speed with corrections attached; they never forgive discovering one themselves.

Walk the statutory risk. The 19th, VAT due the 21st, and the client hasn't answered the query that determines ₦500,000 of output VAT. This one escalates INSIDE first (reviewer + books manager, today) because the decision — file on best evidence vs file late — is a management call with penalty mathematics attached; the client message then carries the firm's decision, not your improvisation.

The invariant: the client must never learn of a problem from a red cell, a silent gap, or their own discovery. The board's surfaces are fast; you must be faster, and the difference between "they told me before I asked" and "I found out" is, over a few years, the difference between a reference and a churn.

DRILL: Which is worse: statements two days late and announced on day one, or one day late and silent? — Silent, and it isn't close. Lateness costs a day; silence costs the belief that you'd tell them. The entire acknowledgment/ceremony machinery is built on that belief.

lessons.title: Review — both chairs, with a worked exchange
lessons.html:
On split clients one prepares, one signs. Here is a real review cycle done well, then the crafts named.

The submission (you, preparer): Cascade July → In Review, notes: "Checklist 6/7. Flux notes in the cell. Two things for your eye: (1) director loan repostings wk3 — I followed his email but the pattern's new; (2) COGS +18% — I've verified Kolawole's price letter, but the margin drop deserves your read before it reaches the MD." — The craft: review-ready state (suspense zero, notes written) plus your own doubts flagged, not buried. A preparer who surfaces doubts is trusted more; a reviewer who finds an UNFLAGGED known-issue trusts everything less, permanently.

The findings (Ade, reviewer): "Two findings. (1) Rent release doubled — March's reversal missing; fix and re-lay the P&L (this also resolves half your COGS-margin worry: ₦200k of it isn't COGS at all, it's the rent error's shadow in the comparative). (2) Director loan treatment is right, but add his email to the Hub as support. Everything else clean — the flux notes are exactly what the MD conversation needs." — The craft: findings with REASONS and locations ("March's reversal"), teaching not verdicts; credit where due; the fix's downstream effect traced. Compare the useless version: "redo the rent figures and tidy the loan section."

The response (you): fix, re-lay, re-file, one line back: "Both done — reversal posted (JE-00318), P&L re-laid, email filed. Re-review when ready." Never relitigate the fact of being checked; argue the ACCOUNTING when you disagree ("I read the pro-ration differently — here's the contract clause") and accept the outcome when the reviewer holds.

The signature (Ade): reviewer-pass tick, Delivered. That click means "I believe these statements" — which is why review is substance (recs to statements, controls to schedules, flux against knowledge of the client) and never a checklist skim. And it is PROMPT: work at In Review since the 3rd deserves better than a signature on the 7th; the 👁 push exists so the handover never waits on memory.

The culture line: the gate only works if being reviewed carries no shame and reviewing carries no superiority. The best pairs swap findings like colleagues sharpening each other — because that is what they are. And the SM override on the gate is for genuine emergencies; a pattern of overrides is a pattern management reads correctly.

DRILL: As reviewer you find a third consecutive month of the same suspense-hygiene issue from the same preparer. The finding goes in the review — where else does the observation belong? A direct conversation (kind, specific, offline from the artifact) — findings fix statements; conversations fix patterns. If a third conversation doesn't, the books manager should hear it from you before the KPIs say it anyway.

lessons.title: Your numbers — reading the board without flinching
lessons.html:
The board measures the work: on-time rate, posting lags, close cycles, register dots, and (for managers) each engagement's effective hourly rate. Professionals read their own numbers the way they read a client's: honestly, hunting the story. A sample read:

Your six-month row: on-time 94% → 91% → 96% → 88% → 90% → 84%. FS cycle: 4.2d → 4.5d → 4.1d → 5.8d → 5.5d → 6.3d. The story isn't "getting worse at the job" — cross-reference capacity: you went from 3 clients to 5 in month four. The honest conclusion is a LOAD conversation with the books manager, armed with the numbers ("my cycle degraded exactly when the portfolio grew — I'm at capacity, or my rhythm needs redesign, or both"). The board wrote your case for you; that is what it's for.

The two corruptions, named: Gaming — attesting optimistically, back-dating effort, ticking unverified — poisons the board for everyone and is a short strategy against a system whose cross-checks (sessions vs claims, batch vs schedule, and one day the ledger itself) have a long memory. Despair — treating an amber month as a verdict — misreads what the numbers are: descriptions of the service each client received, nothing more. The correct response to a bad number is curiosity (what in my rhythm produced this?) followed by a changed rhythm.

The fee-review flag, understood precisely: when an engagement runs below the rate floor three straight months, the CLIENT is flagged — for repricing, not for blame. It means the engagement is bigger than the fee assumed. Your honest hours are the evidence that makes the repricing case; understating hours to look efficient literally hides money the unit should be earning. The flag firing is the pricing system WORKING.

Capacity and growth: the lightest-honest-load table assigns the next client; disciplined numbers are how growth lands fairly, and how your advancement case gets written by the board instead of by adjectives. The closing loop of this whole track: tag sessions, attest truly, raise queries the day you hit them, tick what you verified — do the disciplines and the KPIs take care of themselves. That is the design.

DRILL: Your Cascade rate reads ₦3,900/hr for the third month; the flag fires. A colleague suggests logging fewer Cascade hours "so it looks better". Name the three things wrong with that in one breath: it hides an underpriced engagement (unit loses money), corrupts capacity planning (you'll be assigned MORE work), and it's a falsified record in a system built on attestation. The right move: nothing — the flag is doing your negotiating for you.

lessons.title: Pressure — when a client asks for a particular answer
lessons.html:
Everything so far assumes you and the client want the same thing. Occasionally you will not, and this is the chapter for that day.

What it actually sounds like. Almost never falsify this. It arrives as reasonable-sounding requests, usually from somebody under real strain: can that sit in next month instead; treat the generator as a repair rather than an asset; my personal card bill went through the business, just put it to entertainment; leave the stock at last month's figure, the count was rushed. Each has a version that is legitimate and a version that is not, which is exactly what makes them hard.

The distinction that resolves most of them. Is this a judgement with a defensible basis, or a preference for a different answer? Cut-off, capitalisation and estimation are genuine judgements with rules behind them — and where the rules permit a range, the client's view is a legitimate input. Moving a transaction to a different month because the month looks better is not a judgement; it is a different answer, chosen for its appearance.

The three-step response, in order.

Understand it first. Help me understand the reasoning — what's driving that? A surprising share of these turn out to be genuine and correctly argued, and you will have learned something about the business. Refusing before understanding is how a bookkeeper becomes somebody the client stops telling things to.

Say what you can and cannot do, without judgement of them. I can't move a July transaction into August — the date is the date. What I can do is show it clearly in the flux note so the month reads properly. Naming the alternative matters: a flat no leaves them with the problem they started with.

Escalate rather than negotiate. If it does not resolve there, it stops being yours. Let me take this to the books manager and come back to you today. That is not passing the difficulty upward to avoid it — the firm holds the relationship and the professional exposure, and a bookkeeper who settles these alone is carrying something that was never theirs.

What you never do, whatever the pressure. Post something you believe to be wrong. Backdate a document to a period that has closed. Delete rather than reverse. Or agree verbally and hope it is forgotten — the request will be repeated next month, and the second refusal is harder than the first would have been.

And the thing worth understanding about the person asking. They are usually not trying to make you complicit. They are under a bank covenant, a tax deadline, or a partner's question, and they have asked the person nearest the numbers. Treating it as an ordinary request handled firmly, rather than as an accusation, is what keeps the relationship intact through the refusal.

lessons.title: Suspicion — what you must not ignore
lessons.html:
Rarely, something in the books is not a bookkeeping question. This chapter is about recognising that moment and what to do in the first hour, and it is deliberately narrow: your job is to notice and to tell one person, not to investigate or decide.

What the shape looks like. Round-sum transfers to parties with no invoices and no obvious business purpose. Payments to a name that does not appear anywhere else in the client's affairs. Cash movements that do not fit the trade. A pattern of transactions just below a threshold. Instructions to route money through an account for no stated reason. Any of these can be entirely innocent and explained in a sentence — most are — which is precisely why the response is a question rather than a conclusion.

Ordinary curiosity first. Raise it as you would any unclassifiable item: a query, help-shaped, same day. Most of what looks odd resolves there, and a bookkeeper who escalates everything unusual is one nobody can work with.

When the answer does not resolve it. The answer does not fit the transaction, or the question is deflected, or the explanation changes. That is the moment this chapter is about, and from there the rules are firm.

Tell the named person in the firm, once, in writing, the same day. Your firm has somebody who holds this — a partner, a compliance owner, the books manager. Find out who before you need to, because looking it up during the hour it matters is not the moment.

Then four things you do not do. Do not confront the client or challenge them about it. Do not investigate — no digging through old periods, no assembling evidence, no calling the bank. Do not discuss it with colleagues, including the ones you trust. And do not tell the client that you have raised it, which matters more than it sounds: whether and how anything is disclosed is a decision for the firm, and a client who learns a report may be coming is a serious problem for everybody, including you.

Keep working normally unless told otherwise. Changing how you behave toward that client is itself a signal. Post the ordinary transactions, deliver the pack, answer the queries — the firm will tell you if anything changes.

What this module deliberately does not tell you. What your firm's reporting obligations are. Those depend on the firm's registrations and on rules that change, and a track that stated them confidently would eventually be confidently wrong. What does not change is the shape: notice, tell one named person, do not investigate, do not tip off. Ask your firm for the specifics on the day you join, and write down the name.

lessons.title: When it was your mistake
lessons.html:
The bad-news protocol covered a late statement and an error reaching a delivered pack. This is the harder version: the error is yours, you found it, and nobody else knows.

The instinct, and why it is wrong. To fix it quietly and say nothing. It is understandable, it usually works, and it costs you the one thing this job runs on — because the day a quiet fix is discovered, everything else you have ever attested becomes a question. A bookkeeper's value is that their word about the books can be relied on, and that is not divisible.

The protocol, and it is short.

Establish the size before you speak, but not for long. What was wrong, which periods, what it affects. Twenty minutes, not two days — you are describing the problem, not solving it first.

Tell your reviewer or manager, plainly, without cushioning. I posted the March rent release twice; the P&L is overstated by ₦200,000 for March and April. Statements went out for both. That is the whole message. No preamble, no explanation of how it happened until asked, and no apology longer than the facts.

Bring what you propose to do. The correcting entry, whether the client needs a reissued pack or a note, and what would stop it recurring. A mistake reported with a proposal reads completely differently from a mistake reported as a confession.

Then let somebody else decide what the client is told. Whether a pack is reissued, and how it is described, is not yours alone — particularly where the numbers went to a bank or an adviser.

What happens next, honestly. Far less than people fear. Reviewers and managers meet errors constantly; what they remember is how it arrived. The bookkeepers who become trusted are not the ones who never make mistakes — there are none of those — they are the ones whose mistakes arrive early, complete and without excuses.

And the corrections themselves. Reverse and repost, never delete and never edit history. The trail should show the error, the correction and their link, because a corrected ledger that hides its correction is a ledger somebody will one day have to reconstruct without knowing why the figures moved.

What to do when the error is somebody else's. The same, minus the ownership. Tell your reviewer or manager what you found, factually and without characterising the person — the March rent release looks doubled, not somebody double-posted the rent. It is not your place to work out who, and saying so as a finding rather than an accusation is what keeps a unit workable.

The one that is hardest. An error you find months later, in a period nobody is looking at, that nobody would ever notice. The rule is the same and the reason is simpler than ethics: you already know, and the alternative is carrying it.

checks.why: A bookkeeper's value is that their word about the books can be relied on, and that is not divisible.

lessons.title: The limits of your competence
lessons.html:
The most expensive errors in this work are rarely careless. They are a confident answer given by somebody slightly outside what they actually knew, and the whole of this chapter is about recognising that edge in yourself.

Where the edge usually is. Tax treatment beyond the routine. Anything involving a director's personal affairs and the company's. Foreign currency and translation. A transaction structure you have not seen before — a lease that might be a purchase, a related-party arrangement, an unusual instrument. And any question phrased as can we rather than how do I post, which is almost always an advice question wearing bookkeeping clothes.

The tell. You are reasoning by analogy — it is probably like the other one — rather than from a rule you can name. That feeling is reliable, and it is the moment to stop rather than the moment to look harder.

What to do with it, and it is three sentences. I want to check that rather than guess. Take it to whoever holds it in your firm. Come back with the answer and the reasoning, not just the answer, because the reasoning is what you keep.

Saying it to a client. That's a good question and I don't want to give you a quick answer to it — let me check and come back today. Clients do not lose confidence in a bookkeeper who checks. They lose confidence in one who was confident and wrong, and the second is unrecoverable in a way the first never is.

Where the line sits between bookkeeping and advice. Recording what happened is yours. What the client should do about it frequently is not, and the boundary matters both ways — a bookkeeper who advises on tax structure is exposing themselves and the firm, and one who refuses to explain what a figure means is being unhelpful about their own work. Explaining the books is always yours. Recommending a course of action generally is not.

What competence actually grows from. Not from getting things right, which teaches little. From the questions you escalated and the answers that came back — which is why bringing back the reasoning rather than the answer is the whole technique. Bookkeepers who do this for a year know why the rules are as they are; those who ask only for the answer know a list.

The pressure that produces the confident wrong answer. A client on a call, waiting, and a question you half-know. The whole difficulty is that let me check feels like a failure in that specific moment and is forgotten within a day, while a wrong answer is acted on and remembered. Knowing in advance that the discomfort is momentary and the error is durable is most of what it takes to say it.

And the standard, stated once. Nobody expects you to know everything. Everybody is entitled to expect that you know what you do not know, and say so before it matters rather than after.

face.title: Bookkeeper — The Books Face — Screen by Screen
face.desc: Every tab of 📒 Books, button by button: the header and periods, Matrix, My round, Register, Follow-ups, Onboarding — and the manager tabs (Profitability, Billing, KPIs) so you know what the numbers you generate become.

lessons.title: Getting in, the header, and what a period is
lessons.html:
Where the face lives. On desktop, open Duty Board and click 📒 Books in the face navigation. On a phone, it is the 📒 tab in the bottom tab bar. You will see the face only if you are one of: a bookkeeper assigned to at least one accounting client, a books manager, or a System Manager. If you believe you should see it and don't, your name isn't set as any client's bookkeeper yet — that is a one-click fix by whoever manages the matrix (Lesson 2), not a bug.

Where you land. Bookkeepers land on My round; managers land on Matrix. The tab strip across the top reads: Matrix · My round · Register · Follow-ups · Onboarding — and, for managers only: ₦ Profitability · 💰 Billing · 📈 KPIs. If you don't see the last three, you are not missing anything broken; they are gated.

The period selector. In the header sits ‹ 2026-07 › — a month, in YYYY-MM form. This is the single most important control on the face: every tab obeys it simultaneously. Set it to June and the Matrix shows June's deliverables, the Register shows June's grid, Billing shows June's invoice run. You never set it per-tab. Investigating last month means clicking ‹ once, doing all your looking, then clicking › back. Forgetting you're parked on an old month is the #1 cause of "the board looks wrong" — check the selector before you panic.

The pulse strip. Under the header: clients · done/total · late · neglected · 📨 (open questions/requests) — and for managers, the month's fee total and unpaid. Read it left to right as triage: neglected first (a client nobody is touching), late second (a promise already broken), 📨 third (clients waiting on us). The done-count is yesterday's news; it needs no action.

What a period actually is, and how it opens. A period is one calendar month of obligations. When a period "opens", the system creates that month's deliverables for every client — the core set (bank journals, reconciliation, financial statements) plus whatever optional items each client's tier ticks (statutory, stock take in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec only) — each pre-assigned to the client's default bookkeeper, each with its computed due date. It also spawns the month's standard document requests (bank statements etc.) to every client. You never create the month's work; you inherit it.

Opening happens automatically, every day: a scheduled job syncs any newly on-boarded customers and opens the current month — running daily makes it self-healing, so a client on-boarded on the 14th gets their July deliverables that same night. There are also two manual buttons on the Matrix, for staff, for the moments you can't wait for tonight: Sync clients (pull newly On-Board customers into rooms right now) and Open period (create any missing deliverables for the selected period right now). Both are idempotent — clicking them twice, or clicking them after the nightly job already ran, creates nothing twice, ever. So the rule is simple: mid-month new client, or a cell you expected is missing? Click Sync clients, then Open period, and the matrix fills in. Nothing bad can happen from these buttons.

DRILL: It's 2 August. The matrix looks strangely finished and Billing shows nothing generated. Before reporting a bug — what do you check? The period selector: you are almost certainly still parked on July. Click › to August; the fresh month's pending cells appear. If August shows NO cells at all, the nightly open hasn't run yet — click Open period and watch them spawn.

lessons.title: The Matrix — reading it, and the two dialogs behind it
lessons.html:
The Matrix is the unit's scoreboard: one row per client, one column per deliverable type, one period at a time. Proficiency means reading any cell in under a second and knowing exactly what clicking anything does.

The client column (leftmost) carries four things per row: the client's name; the 📮 chip — "posted thru 24-07 · lag 2wd", colored green (lag ≤1 working day), amber (≤3), or red (beyond), or "no attestation" grey if the round has never been run for them; the bookkeeper's first name as a link (or "— set" if unassigned); and the 📖 playbook icon. Managers additionally see the monthly fee here; bookkeepers don't — deliberately.

Clicking the bookkeeper name opens Client setup — the dialog that defines the engagement: Bookkeeper (default owner) — who inherits every new deliverable for this client; and Service tier — optional deliverables this client pays for — a set of checkboxes (PAYE, VAT, WHT, Stock take…). Ticking a tier item means future periods spawn it; unticked means the column shows "—" for this client and it is not our obligation. Change either, Save, and the change applies from the next spawn — existing cells keep their current assignee until you change them individually.

Clicking 📖 opens the playbook — a monospace editor pre-loaded (first time) with four headings: banks & statements, key contacts, month peculiarities, access notes. Read it before your first day on any client; update it the day you learn anything a covering colleague would need; Save. Every unit member can read every playbook — that is its entire purpose.

The deliverable cells, glyph by glyph: · Pending (spawned, untouched) · ◐ In progress · 👁 In review (sitting with the reviewer) · ✓ Delivered · ✓✓ Acknowledged by client · a red cell with ⚠ is past its due date without Delivered — visible to everyone, counted in the pulse, named in the digest. Under each glyph sits the computed due date. Two special marks: ↻ Sep in a quarterly column means subscribed-but-dormant (next live in September); — means not in this client's tier at all. Never confuse those two.

Clicking any cell opens the deliverable dialog, prefilled with current values:

  1. The checklist (financial statements carry one; statutory items don't, by design): tick items as you verify them — each tick stamps your name and time permanently, and the progress bar updates. A tick is a signed statement that you checked that thing this month.
  2. Status — Pending → In Progress → (In Review) → Delivered. Setting In Review pushes a 👁 notification to the reviewer. Setting Delivered: if a Reviewer is named on the cell, only that reviewer (or a System Manager) can select it — anyone else is refused by name. Delivered fires the ceremony: the client's room announces the deliverable, and their portal shows the 📬 Confirm-receipt card. If checklist items are still open, you'll be asked "deliver anyway?" — allowed, but the unticked items stay visible forever, so justify any override in Notes.
  3. Assigned to — reassignable per cell (coverage, load-balancing) without touching the client's default.
  4. Reviewer (split clients) — naming one arms the review gate on this cell.
  5. Notes — flux sentences, doubts flagged for the reviewer, override justifications. Write here as if the reader is a stranger in six months, because eventually they will be.

✓✓ can never be set by staff. Acknowledged exists only when the client themselves taps Confirm receipt — which is exactly what makes it proof of delivery.

DRILL: A cell shows 👁 and the due date is tomorrow. What do you (the preparer) do — and not do? Do: nothing to the cell; nudge the reviewer directly if the push hasn't moved them, and escalate to a manager early tomorrow if needed. Don't: change Status yourself, and never remove the Reviewer to free the Delivered option — that edit is logged and reads exactly as it is.

lessons.title: My round — the daily attestation, field by field
lessons.html:
Once per working day, for each of your clients, you record where their books stand. The tab shows one card per client assigned to you (if it says "No accounting clients assigned to you", the Matrix's Client setup hasn't named you yet).

Reading a card before you touch it: the client's name; a ● or ○ — ● means a Work Session tagged to this customer exists today (you visibly worked them), ○ means none yet; a green ✓ attested once you've saved today's entry; and on the right, the current claim — "posted thru 2026-07-24 · lag 2wd" in the same green/amber/red as the matrix chip, or "no attestation yet".

The four fields and the save:

  1. The date picker — the posted-through date: the latest date for which every transaction dated up to and including it is in the client's ledger. The picker physically stops at today, and the server refuses future dates independently — you cannot have posted tomorrow's transactions. If you posted through Wednesday and it's Thursday, you enter Wednesday: the lag chip may show amber, and that is fine. The chip is allowed to be amber; the attestation is not allowed to be false.
  2. tx posted — roughly how many transactions you posted today. An estimate is fine; it gives the digest texture.
  3. queries — how many client questions you raised today. This field exists to remind you that raising queries the day you hit them is part of the day's work, not month-end's.
  4. note (optional) — one line of context: "creditor analysis for MD; postings current to 14-07", "6 late-arriving 21-07 tx posted on receipt of statement page". Use it especially on days when the date doesn't move — an unchanged date with a note is honest; a skipped attestation is a hole.

Press 💾. You'll see the green "Attested" toast, the card gains ✓ attested, and the header pulse refreshes. Saving again the same day updates today's entry — posted further this afternoon? Re-attest with the later date; no duplicate is created.

The three commandments of the round: (1) run it for every client, every working day — including clients you didn't touch (their card simply keeps yesterday's date; the Register still needs the honesty of the gap, and Lesson 4 shows what two silent days look like); actually no — precisely: attest the clients you worked; the ones you didn't touch stay silent and the Register records that truthfully. What you never do is skip attesting a client you DID work. (2) Fixed time daily — 16:30 is a good ritual; a round run "when I remember" is a round not run. (3) The date is a claim with your name on it, forever. Nothing on this board matters more than that claim staying true.

DRILL: Your card shows ○ (no session today) but you spent two hours on this client this morning. What went wrong, and why does it matter? You forgot to clock a Work Session tagged to the customer — so the Register will show ◔ (claim without visible presence) when you attest, profitability undercounts the engagement's hours, and capacity thinks you're free. Clock the session (even now), then attest. Untagged work might as well not have happened.

lessons.title: The Register and the digest — how the unit sees itself
lessons.html:
🗓 Register renders the selected month as a grid: one row per client, one column per working day (weekends and non-workdays simply absent). Each cell is one of four marks:

  1. ● — a customer-tagged Work Session exists that day and an attestation was saved. The complete day.
  2. ◐ — worked (session exists) but no attestation. You did the job and skipped the ritual — finish it; today's entry can still be saved today.
  3. ◔ — attested but no session. A claim with no visible presence behind it. Occasionally legitimate (you attested an unchanged date on a no-work day with a note); as a pattern, it invites exactly the question you'd expect.
  4. · — untouched: no session, no attestation.

The neglect rule: a client with 2 or more consecutive silent working days (no session, no attestation) turns the whole row red and shows the streak — "3wd" — beside the client's name. Nothing else happens automatically: no reassignment, no lock, no manager alarm. What happens instead is the digest.

The 18:00 digest, every working day, lands with every bookkeeper and every books manager — the same message for all: which clients were covered today (and by whom), which were partial (◐/◔), which untouched, which are neglected with their streaks and names, plus what's currently awaiting clients (open questions/documents). Read yours daily even when your rows are clean — it is how you know when a colleague needs cover before anyone has to ask.

What this system is and isn't: it is deliberate peer visibility — the theory is that a small professional unit keeps itself honest when everyone sees everything, so there is no escalation machinery hiding behind it. It is not surveillance: nobody is timing your keystrokes; the only thing measured is whether each client's books have a visible, attested heartbeat. Keep the heartbeat and the Register never thinks about you.

DRILL: Thursday's digest shows Cascade at "2wd" under your name — you were consumed by a Bellamy fire Tuesday–Wednesday. What's the recovery, precisely? Thursday: clock a Cascade session, clear the backlog to wherever is TRUE (maybe only through Tuesday), attest that true date with a note. The streak clears; the lag chip may sit amber a day; the scar in the Register stays, honestly, and that's fine. What you don't do: attest "through Thursday" to make it all look green — the register would show ● but the claim would be false, and false is the one thing this board cannot absorb.

Why the register is monthly rather than a running list. Because the pattern is the point. A single missed day tells nobody anything; a row with three gaps in a fortnight is a conversation about capacity or about a client who has become difficult to work. Reading it monthly means the conversation happens while it is still about workload rather than about performance.

What to do with your own row. Read it before your manager does. A row with an obvious explanation — leave, a client on hold, a week of onboarding — is worth a sentence in the digest note rather than a question later. The register is not an accusation, and it becomes one only when it is the manager who notices first.

lessons.title: Follow-ups — questions, documents, and everything the system chases for you
lessons.html:
📨 Follow-ups is where you turn "I can't post this" and "I don't have that" into structured items the system tracks, chases, and files. The tab has a client filter (All clients dropdown — narrow it when working one client), two creation buttons, three lists.

➕ New question — for a transaction you can't classify. Fields: the client, the transaction date, the amount, the reference (the statement narration — "CHQ 000451 MUSA ENT"), and your question, phrased help-shaped: "Could you help us place this cheque to Musa Ent on the 9th?" On save, two things happen at once: an amber card appears on the client's portal home with an inline answer box, and an email goes to the client from the books mailbox. The client can answer either way — typing in the card, or simply replying to the email; a reply is captured, the quoted chain trimmed, and filed as the answer with their name on it. You do not care which path they choose; both land identically.

➕ New request — for a document you need. Fields: client, title ("June GTB statement, pages 3–4"), due date. The client sees a green upload card and gets the email; they fulfil by portal upload or by replying with the file attached — either way the file lands automatically in their Document Hub under "Accounting — received", the request closes itself, and the room announces it. Note also: the standard monthly set (bank statements and whatever else is configured) is raised automatically for every client when the period opens — you only create requests for the ad-hoc extras.

The Questions list shows each item with its age in working days: open (amber — waiting on the client) or answered (green — the client has responded; their answer text is right there). Your move on green: act on the answer in the ledger (repost the suspense to its true account), then press Resolve. Open → Answered → Resolved is the full life; a query left at Answered is work you've forgotten, and Lesson M2b calls an Answered-unresolved item at close what it is — a landmine with a polite label.

The Document requests list: outstanding items with due dates (overdue in red). Waive is for requests genuinely no longer needed (the client sent it inside another file; the month closed without it mattering) — waiving records that decision rather than leaving a phantom chase running.

📥 Recently received: the latest documents clients have sent, newest first, each with an Open link — check it each morning; it is faster than asking "did they send it yet".

The chase you never send: every working morning at 9:30, any client with items stale 2+ working days (or requests past due) gets one gentle reminder in their room — one per client per day maximum, no matter how many items wait, and (since v2.94) the same single message also carries any overdue service-invoice reminder. Your persistence is automated, bounded, and polite; your job is only to raise items the day you hit them so the machine has something to chase early instead of everything to chase late.

DRILL: Monday: you raise a question on a ₦150,000 unknown credit. Wednesday 9:30 passes. What has the client experienced, in order — and what have you had to remember? Monday: amber card + email. Wednesday morning: one room reminder (2wd stale). You have had to remember: nothing. Thursday the client replies to the email; the question turns green in your list with their answer attached; you repost Suspense → the true account and press Resolve. Total items tracked in your head across four days: zero.

lessons.title: Onboarding — bringing a new client live
lessons.html:
When a new customer is marked On Board and the sync creates their room, the system also spawns their onboarding runbook — the step list that takes them from "signed" to "first month running". The 🚀 Onboarding tab shows every client currently mid-runbook; clients with no started steps show Not started with a Start onboarding button.

The steps come from the configured template (or the 9-step default): the kickoff call, bank read-only access obtained and registered in the Access Register, ERP roles confirmed, opening balances agreed, the playbook's first draft written, the standard monthly requests explained to the client, the first period opened, tier confirmed against the signed engagement, and the welcome message in the room. Each step is a checkbox: tick it when it is actually done — every tick stamps your name and time, and the client's progress bar advances. The ticks are the audit trail of how the engagement began; eighteen months later, "who obtained bank access and when" is a lookup, not an archaeology dig.

The final tick narrates — the room announces onboarding complete, which the client sees. From that moment the client is simply a normal row on the Matrix with a normal monthly rhythm.

Two disciplines while onboarding: first, the access steps and the register are one motion — access obtained but unregistered is an audit finding waiting to happen (and the quarterly review will surface it). Second, the playbook step is not a formality: the person onboarding a client knows things — statement quirks discovered on the kickoff call, who the real decision-maker is — that will cost the next person days to rediscover. Write them down while they're cheap.

DRILL: A new client's runbook shows 7/9 with "bank access registered" unticked, but you know access was obtained — you've been posting from their statements for a week. What's actually wrong, and what do you do? The access exists but was never entered in the Duty Access Register — the tick is unticked because the REGISTRATION is genuinely undone. Create the register entry (type, detail, granted date), then tick the step. The step was telling the truth; listen to it.

Why onboarding is a runbook rather than a checklist in somebody's head. Because it happens rarely enough that nobody is fluent in it. A bookkeeper does perhaps three a year, each some months apart, and the steps most often skipped are the ones with no immediate consequence — the playbook first draft, the standard monthly requests explained. Those are exactly the ones that cost a year of small friction when missed.

The step that is worth doing properly whatever the hurry. Opening balances agreed. Everything after it inherits whatever was accepted, and a balance agreed loosely at onboarding is a difference somebody hunts at the first reconciliation, the first control tie and the first year end. Agreed means agreed in writing with the client, not accepted from a spreadsheet.

lessons.title: Profitability (₦) — what managers see about each engagement
lessons.html:
The last three tabs are manager-gated: ₦ Profitability, 💰 Billing, 📈 KPIs. You may not see them today — this lesson and the next two exist so you understand what your daily discipline turns into, because every number on these screens is built from what bookkeepers record, and some of you will hold the manager view sooner than you think.

What the tab shows: one row per client for the selected period: the monthly fee (from the customer record), the hours of customer-tagged Work Sessions logged against them that month, and the division — the effective hourly rate, ₦/hr. Sorted worst-first, with rates below the configured floor (Duty Settings, default ₦5,000/hr) in red. A client with a fee but no tagged hours shows "—": unmeasurable, which is its own finding.

What the number means — and doesn't. A red rate does not say "the bookkeeper is slow". It says the engagement consumes more hours than its fee assumed — messy source documents, a chatty MD, a business that outgrew its price. The tab exists to surface repricing conversations while they're calm, not to grade people. Conversely, a suspiciously high rate with tiny hours usually means under-tagging, not efficiency — which starves this tab, the Register, and capacity planning all at once.

Your part in it, as a bookkeeper: exactly one thing — tag every Work Session with its customer, honestly. Log the real hours including the annoying parts; the annoying parts are precisely what justifies the repricing. Understating hours to look fast literally hides money the unit should be earning — the KPI lesson shows how the system eventually turns three months of honest hours into an automatic fee-review flag.

DRILL: Your manager mentions your smallest client shows ₦12,000/hr while your biggest shows ₦3,800/hr. Translate both numbers into what they're actually saying. The small client is priced comfortably (or you under-tag them — check); the big one is consuming hours far beyond its fee — a repricing candidate. Neither number is about your speed; both are about the fee fitting the work.

What the rate does not mean. That a bookkeeper is slow. An engagement can read red because the fee was set before anybody knew the volume, because the client is genuinely difficult, or because onboarding hours landed in one month. The number opens a conversation about the engagement rather than about the person, and reading it any other way makes people log fewer hours — which destroys the only measurement the unit has.

Why hours must be tagged to be counted. An untagged session is invisible to this screen. That is not a rule for the manager's benefit: it is the mechanism by which an underpriced engagement becomes provable, and a bookkeeper who does not tag their hours is the one with no evidence when the load conversation comes.

lessons.title: Billing (💰) — how the month becomes an invoice
lessons.html:
The automatic run: on the 28th of each month at 07:00, the system drafts one Sales Invoice per accounting client — the monthly fee as a line item, VAT applied from the configured tax template, due date per the configured terms. This happens regardless of delivery status — that is deliberate policy: the fee is for the service month, and delivery timing is a separate conversation. The drafts are exactly that — drafts: a human reviews and submits them in the Sales Invoice list; nothing is ever sent to a client unreviewed.

The tab, top to bottom: the period's run status — how many drafts await review ("Draft — review & submit"), how many are Unpaid, Paid, or show "no fee set" (a client whose customer record lacks a fee: they were silently skipped, which is the first thing to fix); a Generate now button for running the current period manually (safe at any time — an idempotency marker means a client is never invoiced twice for the same period, so Generate now after the cron, or twice in a row, creates nothing extra); and the Awaiting payment table — client, invoice number, outstanding amount, due date, with days-overdue in red. The pulse strip's unpaid count and total come from here.

The gentle collections you never do: once an invoice is submitted and slips past due, the morning chase adds a courteous payment line to that client's single daily reminder — first working day overdue, then every third — scoped strictly to accounting-service invoices, never any other invoice the wider business raises. Managers watch the Awaiting table; nobody composes dunning messages.

Your part as a bookkeeper: almost nothing, by design — except understanding the client's view: on the 28th-ish they receive an invoice; if it goes unpaid past due they'll see soft reminders in the same room you work in. If a client mentions their invoice to you, the answer is warm and simple — "our team handles billing; I'll flag it for them today" — plus an actual flag to a manager. Never negotiate, discount, or explain fee structure yourself; that's a management lane.

DRILL: It's the 29th; a manager says a client's draft never appeared. The two likeliest causes, in checking order? (1) No fee on the customer record — the tab's "no fee set" list confirms in one glance. (2) An invoice for this period already exists (draft or submitted) from an earlier manual run — the idempotency marker correctly refused a duplicate. Only after those: check the scheduler ran.

Why billing runs on the 28th regardless. The fee is for the service month and delivery timing is a separate conversation — which sounds harsh and protects everybody. A run conditional on delivery would make an invoice into a scorecard, put pressure on the close, and give a client the impression that a late pack is a discount negotiation. Delivery problems are handled as delivery problems.

What to check before submitting the drafts. The no-fee list first, because those clients were silently skipped and will be invisible until somebody notices the revenue is short. Then any client whose fee changed mid-month, since the draft carries the customer record's current figure rather than what was agreed for the period.

lessons.title: KPIs (📈) — what six months of discipline looks like
lessons.html:
The KPI tab is the unit's memory: everything the daily rituals record, compounded into trend. Manager-gated — but the numbers are about the work you do, so know them.

The trend table — the last six periods as columns: deliverables done/total; on-time rate (delivered on or before due, as a % of delivered — green ≥90, amber ≥70, red below); FS close cycle — how many days after month-end the financial statements actually went out, the single number that summarises the practice (the promise is ≤5 working days); and average posting lag — the mean gap, in working days, between attested posted-through dates and the days they were attested. Every one of these is computed from cells you moved and attestations you saved.

Per client over the same window: done/total, on-time %, FS cycle, posting lag — plus client ack latency: how many days the client takes to tap Confirm receipt. That last one quietly identifies who actually reads what we send — useful before proposing anything to them.

Per bookkeeper: delivered count, on-time %, open-this-period. Yes, it is a comparison table; that is why it lives behind the gate. Read your own numbers the way you'd read a client's — as description, not verdict: a cycle that degraded exactly when your portfolio grew from three clients to five is a load story, and the numbers argue your case better than adjectives ever will.

🚩 Fee review: any client whose effective ₦/hr ran below the floor for three consecutive months is flagged automatically, all three rates shown. This is Profitability's snapshot become policy: the flag opens a repricing conversation with evidence attached. It fires because your tagged hours were honest — which is why gaming them backwards (fewer hours to "look efficient") sabotages the exact mechanism that right-sizes your workload's price.

👜 Capacity: per bookkeeper — clients owned, deliverables open now, average tagged hours/month over the trailing quarter — sorted lightest-first, with the next-client suggestion highlighted. When client #7 signs, this table decides who takes them. Honest numbers are how growth lands fairly; that is the closing loop of everything this track teaches: tag sessions, attest truly, raise queries same-day, tick what you verified — and every screen in this lesson takes care of itself.

DRILL: The trend shows on-time 96% but FS cycle drifting 4.1 → 5.2 → 5.9 days. What's the story, and why does it matter before it breaks? Deliveries are still inside the promise but each month closer to the edge — the buffer is eroding (rising volume, or a slow client's documents). It matters now because at 6.1 the on-time number cliff-drops; the drift was the warning, and drift is exactly what a six-column table exists to show.
